page.title: The quickjs sandbox · tinyactors guides
page.description: Run charts you did not write in QuickJS, a separate engine with no I/O and limits on time and memory.

hero.headline: Run charts you did not write.
hero.lede: The quickjs datamodel runs chart code in a separate engine, with no I/O and limits on time and memory.

section.heading: Pick a datamodel per host.
section.p: A host runs all its charts on one of two datamodels, and both take the same charts.

item.text: Chart code runs in node:vm contexts of your own engine, fast and with your engine's values. A vm context is not a security boundary: a chart can reach the process it runs in.
Chart code runs in QuickJS, an engine compiled into the package, with no modules, timers, files or network, and limits on how long an evaluation runs and how much memory it takes.

section.p: Use quickjs for charts you did not write: charts your users upload, or charts a program generates.

section.heading: A runaway evaluation ends in an error.
section.p: This chart loops forever, allocates forever and looks for Node.js. Each runaway evaluation ends in error.execution, and the actor goes on with its next event.

example.code: stopped: error.execution stopped: error.execution undefined undefined undefined

section.heading: Bound each evaluation's work and memory.
section.p: The host's quickjs option sets the limits, with datamodel: 'quickjs' only. With the native datamodel the option is a TypeError.

row.cell: the engine's interrupt checks one evaluation may make before it is stopped
bytes for the whole engine, every actor of the host together
bytes of native stack for JavaScript
'isolated' gives every actor a context of its own (Realms)

section.p: The default memoryLimit stops a runaway allocation at 1 GiB instead of letting it take the process. That fits tens of thousands of resident actors: 40,000 take about 112 MB of engine heap.
A host that keeps more actors resident sets a larger limit. For charts you did not write, set both limits as small as their real work allows.
maxOps counts interrupt checks, one for every 10,000 jumps and calls, not time. How long a check takes depends on the code between checks:

table.caption: How long one looping evaluation holds the host, and every host of its thread. Measured 2026-10-18 on an Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, Linux; Node.js 22 and Bun 1.4.1 alike.

section.p: With the default, one runaway evaluation stalls the thread's hosts for minutes. Choose maxOps by the longest stall your other actors can take:

item.text: a few hundred, 5 to 50 ms, for a service that answers requests;
about 1000, 25 to 250 ms, for background work;
never less than your charts' real work needs: an evaluation that needs more checks fails every time.

section.p: The actor's error.execution says which limit stopped it: _event.data.reason is 'fuel' for maxOps and 'memory' for memoryLimit.
host.quickjsHeapBytes is the engine's heap, every actor's together, to watch against memoryLimit. It is undefined on a native host and once the host is closed.

section.heading: Shared builtins, or a realm each.
section.p: By default the actors of a chart share one context, each a small scope object, as on the native datamodel. A chart whose scripts declare top-level names gives each actor a context instead.

The shared context's globals are frozen, but its builtins are shared: a chart that changes Array.prototype changes it for every actor. With realm: 'isolated' every actor gets its own context, at the cost of its memory.

section.heading: Three edges differ from native.
section.p: A chart observes the same SCXML on both datamodels. Only hibernation, values and costs differ:

item.text: QuickJS writes its own values into the blob, so a Date, Map, Set, typed array or graph with cycles comes back. A class's instance comes back as a plain object, and a function in a variable still keeps the actor in memory ().

Event data and spawn params convert to the engine's values and back through the value table. A key holding undefined is dropped and an array's undefined becomes null, where the native datamodel keeps both.
Most operations cost less on quickjs, and an idle actor takes less memory ().
